name: Skull Crusher

claims.text: Closed grip with thumbs wrapped, palms toward the feet; lie on a flat bench with feet firmly on the floor.

quotes.text: Holding a barbell with a closed, pronated grip (palms facing your feet and thumbs wrapped around the bar), lie supine (on your back) on a flat bench with your feet firmly placed on the floor.

claims.text: Press the bar off the chest to straight elbows so it sits above the face.

quotes.text: Slowly press the barbell off your chest, fully extending your elbows until the barbell is positioned directly above your face with your palms still facing towards your feet.

claims.text: Keep the wrists neutral, neither bent forward nor back.

quotes.text: Maintain a neutral wrist position (no flexion or extension at the wrist).

claims.text: Bend only the elbows and lower the bar slowly toward the forehead or slightly behind the head.

quotes.text: Inhale and slowly bend the elbows, lowering the bar in a controlled manner towards your forehead or slightly behind your head while maintaining your neutral wrist position.

claims.text: The upper arms stay vertical as the elbows bend; stop just above the forehead or as soon as the upper arms start to drift back.

quotes.text: Your upper arms should remain vertical to the floor as the elbows bend. Lower the bar until it sits just above your forehead or until you notice the upper arms begin to drift backwards.

claims.text: Keep the elbows shoulder-width apart for the whole set.

quotes.text: Attempt to keep your upper arms vertical to the floor throughout the exercise and keep your elbows shoulder-width apart.
Try to keep the same distance between your elbows throughout the movement.

claims.text: Upper arms drifting back is described as the most common fault; it moves load from the triceps to the shoulder (retailer coaching blog).

quotes.text: Upper arms drifting back: the most common fault, and the one that reduces tricep involvement by shifting the load onto the shoulder.

claims.text: The EZ bar puts the wrists half-way between palms up and palms down, which this source says eases wrist and elbow torque versus a straight bar (mechanism stated, not measured).

quotes.text: The angled grip positions of the EZ bar place the wrists in a semi-supinated position — partway between fully supinated (palms up) and fully pronated (palms down). This immediately reduces the torque placed on the wrist and elbow joint compared to a straight bar

claims.text: Too much weight shows as lost elbow position, bouncing and shoulder compensation; reduce the load until every rep is clean.

quotes.text: Too much weight: manifests as loss of elbow position, bar bouncing, and compensation through the shoulder. Fix: reduce load until all reps are clean, then rebuild gradually.

claims.text: Lie with the head close to the end of the bench; use a close grip on the EZ bar.

quotes.text: Lie down on a bench which your head close to the edge. Hold a EZ bar with a close grip, and lift it up to straight arms over yourself.

claims.text: The lying triceps extension trains the triceps, both extending the elbow and bringing the upper arm down.

quotes.text: The lying triceps extension is a very effective tricep exercise that besides extending your elbow joint also trains the triceps function to bring your upper arm down towards your midline.

claims.text: Add load in small steps: ACSM recommends a 2-10% increase once the current load can be done for one to two reps over the target.

quotes.text: it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number

claims.text: For intermediate to advanced lifters with an eventual emphasis on heavy loads (1-6 RM), ACSM advises a moderate speed of 1-2 seconds up and 1-2 seconds down; the plate uses it only as a drawing convention for tempo.

quotes.text: For intermediate (individuals with approximately 6 months of consistent RT experience) to advanced (individuals with years of RT experience) training
with eventual emphasis on heavy loading (1-6 RM) using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)

claims.text: Across US emergency-department weight-training injuries, the most common mechanism was weights dropping on the person, and 90% involved free weights.

quotes.text: The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%). A large number of injuries occurred with free weights (90.4%).

claims.text: Triceps tendon ruptures are rare; they often come from a forceful eccentric (lowering) contraction or lifting against resistance, and are most often seen in middle-aged men, football players and weightlifters.

quotes.text: Triceps tendon ruptures (TTRs) are rare and often occur as a result of falling on an outstretched hand, forceful eccentric contraction, direct trauma to the elbow, or lifting against resistance. TTRs are most commonly seen in middle-aged men, football players, and weightlifters.

claims.text: A way out: have a spotter when doing skull crushers for the first time, and do not go too heavy too fast, because the weight hovers above the head.

quotes.text: Finally, when doing skull crushers for the first time, it’s a good idea to have a spotter.
But, go too heavy, too fast, and the weight is hovering above your head … you could have issues!

claims.text: Lower the bar over about 3 seconds: this retailer coaching blog asks for a controlled eccentric of two to three seconds, and gives three seconds down as the fix for rushing the lowering.

quotes.text: Skull crushers respond well to a controlled eccentric — two to three seconds down — which increases time under tension and maximises the stimulus on the long head.
quotes.where: How to do skull crushers: what not to do

quotes.text: Fix: three seconds down, controlled at the bottom, press back up.
quotes.where: Common skull crusher mistakes and how to fix them

claims.text: Motra's dumbbell overhead extension page lists elbow joint pain under 'When to Avoid' (applied here to the skull crusher, MECH, as on the LB5 overhead extensions). Used for the elbow row's stop line (R-LB5-2).

quotes.text: Elbow joint pain

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; vertical upper arms, the bar's end point at the forehead and the mistake (upper arms drifting back) all read in the sagittal plane (c4, c5, c7). Elbow width needs the front view, so it stays a text point.
plate.equipment: Flat bench, EZ bar (census ezBar), feet flat on the floor (c1); head near the end of the bench (c10).
plate.start: Supine, feet flat (c1); arms straight, upper arms vertical, bar above the face (c2, c5); wrists neutral (c3).
plate.end: Elbows bent, bar just above the forehead (c4, c5); upper arms still vertical (c5).

checkpoints.label: Upper arms vertical
checkpoints.what: Only the forearms move. The upper arms stay upright.

checkpoints.label: Bar to forehead
checkpoints.what: Bar comes down slowly to just above the forehead or slightly behind the head.

checkpoints.label: Wrists neutral
checkpoints.what: Wrists neither bent back nor curled.

mistake.what: Upper arms drifting back toward the head as the bar comes down.
mistake.why: Strength Shop calls it the most common fault (c7, retailer blog, WEAK), and ACE uses it as the stop signal for the descent (c5).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 1: Strength Shop's "Upper arms drifting back: the most common fault" (c7, WEAK) puts the frequency word on that fault itself, not a list heading read onto one item, so it counts; no other quote gives a frequency word for a skull-crusher fault. Set aside: "one of the most frequently butchered" is about the exercise, not one fault; Gaviria's "often occur as a result of falling on an outstretched hand, forceful eccentric contraction" and "most commonly seen in middle-aged men" (c15) name causes and people for triceps ruptures, not a fault of this exercise; Kerr's "The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person" (c14) is about all weight training; "working skull crusher weight is typically 30–45kg" is a load. Step 2 is not needed: Strength Shop's "any lateral drift in the bar exacerbates elbow and wrist strain" ties a sideways bar drift to strain, but no frequency word backs it; too much weight (c9) and a straight bar (c8) are load and equipment choices, not candidates. drawable stays true: the side view shows the upper-arm angle.

tempo.text: 3 s down: the only value in both of Strength Shop's lines for this exercise (c17, WEAK, retailer blog; ruling R-LB2-1). 1 s up keeps ACSM's 1-2 s, stated for intermediate to advanced training (c13, WEAK; LR-15). Pause 0: no quote asks for a pause right after the press; Strength Shop's "Squeeze the triceps at the top" gives no pause or seconds. Fit Father's "Once the bar touches your forehead, pause for 2-3 seconds." is a pause at another point of the rep (the bottom), with the bar on the forehead; it contradicts ACE's stop just above the forehead (c5), so no bottom pause is drawn and pause stays 0.

plate.variantLine: exercises.json lists "EZ Bar / Barbell". The EZ bar is drawn (census ezBar; StrengthLog uses it, c10). The setup, arm path and wrist rules (c1-c6) come from ACE's barbell version and hold for both; the EZ bar's easier wrist angle (c8) is the only difference.

grip.type: Closed grip, palms toward the feet (c1); on the EZ bar the hands sit on the angled inner grips (c8).
grip.width: Close grip (c10), elbows kept shoulder-width apart (c6).
grip.handContact: Not stated by the sources read; no hand-placement rule is given.

setup.step: Lie on a flat bench, head near the end, feet flat.
Grip the bar closed, thumbs wrapped, palms toward your feet.
Press to straight arms above your face. Upper arms vertical.
When new to the lift, have a spotter and start light.
Beat target by one or two reps? Add 2 to 10 percent.

handlingMistakes.fix: Keep them vertical. Stop the descent when they start to move.
Reduce the load until every rep is clean.

rows.means: Fault: upper arms drift back, shifting the load onto the shoulder.

rows.fix: Stop the set. Don't train through the pain.

risks.risk: Bar over the face: wrap the thumbs, lower slowly, have a spotter when new.
Triceps tendon rupture (rare), often from forceful lowering or lifting against resistance.

zooms.right: Thumbs wrapped, wrists straight on the EZ grips.
zooms.wrong: Wrists bent back under the bar.

zooms.right: Upper arms vertical, only the forearms move.
zooms.wrong: Upper arms drifted back toward the head.

libraryDiff.why: exercises.json: triceps primary, no secondary. c11 supports it. No change.

gaps: tier-A way out: the read sources give only a spotter for a first-time lifter; no source says how to end a failed rep without one (LIB-WAYOUT)
